newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Nazi experiment victims mark pogrom in Vienna.
newsitem.headline: Nazi experiment victims mark pogrom in Vienna.

text.p: Jewish Holocaust veterans used as human guinea pigs by Nazi doctor Josef Mengele will relate their experiences for the first time in Austria to mark the anniversary of the 1938 "Crystal Night" pogrom.

Vera Alexander, Otto Klein, Ephraim Reichenberg and Solomon Malek will speak on Sunday at Vienna's progressive Volkstheater about their memories of the twin Auschwitz-Birkenau concentration camps in Poland, where they spent part of World War Two and saw family members killed.

The theatre annually invites speakers to commemorate the night of November 9, 1938 known as "Kristallnacht" when Adolf Hitler's Nazis smashed and looted thousands of Jewish shops and burned synagogues across Germany and Austria.

Mengele, nicknamed the "Angel of Death", performed hundreds of gruesome medical experiments on twins, gypsies and dwarfs at Auschwitz between 1943 and 1944, in an effort to find clues to producing a German master race.

Ephraim Reichenberg, now 70, told Reuters how he and his twin brother were whisked away, aged 17, on arrival at Birkenau to Mengele's laboratory. His mother, father and other seven brothers were sent straight to the gas chambers.
The doctor was keen to find out why Reichenberg's brother had a beautiful singing voice and he did not, he said.
"Every week we had lots of injections and our throats swelled up. We would be sick and lie in bed with fever. Then two days later he (Mengele) would begin again," he said.
Reichenberg and his brother both lost their voices permanently as a result of Mengele's investigations. His twin died of cancer a year after the Allies liberated the camp.
After two years in hospital and some 20 operations, Reichenberg was again able to speak with a special microphone pressed against his voice box. He now lives in Israel.
"A Jew was nothing more to Mengele than a piece of dust," he said. "We were fighting for our lives minute by minute, hour by hour."
Vera Alexander, 75, who also emigrated to Israel after the war, was put in charge of a barracks of twins and gypsies set aside for Mengele's medical research.

She described how a pair of three-year-old gypsy twins were brought back from the operating table having been sown together back to back. "Even the guard on duty cried when he saw the children whining like wounded animals," she said.
"It was done out of sadism, this was no experiment," she added.
Of over 1,000 twins who came under Mengele's scalpel, some 180 survived, according to the veterans.
Alexander also watched Mengele decide the fate of thousands of inmates, as part of Hitler's elimination programme.

All those he sent to the left were to be gassed while those sent to the right were temporarily spared. "He was very good-looking and he would whistle arias from the opera while he selected people for the gas chamber," she said.
All four veterans still bear the tattoos of their inmate numbers. They say the mental and physical scars from the war will never disappear.
"I don't want to remember but I am always dreaming that I am in Auschwitz with my two sons," says Alexander.

Mengele was believed to have escaped to Argentina after the war, but was never found. He was tried in a symbolic trial in Jerusalem in 1985 and found guilty of crimes against humanity and against the Jewish people.
